name: Hookline Independent Dock & Haul Street Kit
description: Not company-issued — this is the working kit of an independent dock laborer, day-hire cargo handler, or gig-economy freight mover who doesn't work for any single corponation long enough to get a uniform. It's assembled from a mix of quality street-label and surplus, and it holds together through deliberate choice rather than institutional supply. The outer layer is a surplus-style work jacket in faded navy waxed cotton, hood stuffed into the collar, with chest pockets reinforced by street-sewn bar tacks. Across the left sleeve, someone has stenciled a small orange triangle with a number — a dock lot designation, or a crew mark, or a union section ID. The jacket's back panel has been slit along the spine and re-laced with industrial paracord to create a crude but effective spinal-rig accommodation channel. Underneath is a heavyweight charcoal henley with three-button placket, thick enough to function as a mid-layer without a separate underlayer. Trousers are navy canvas work pants cut wide in the thigh for movement, with external knee pad channels (pads currently in), cargo pockets on both legs, and a reinforced seat. A wide webbing belt with a heavy D-ring carries a hook tool, a clip for a work lamp, and a battered multi-use utility holster. Boots are thick-soled dock walkers with steel toe and side-zip entry, scuffed to grey at the toe caps. A knit balaclava worn pulled back as a thick watch cap covers the head, grey with a single faded orange stripe.
functionality: Spinal-rig accommodation channel (laced back panel), knee pad channels for prolonged kneeling work, D-ring belt for tool and lamp carry, wide-thigh cut for heavy lifting mobility, side-zip boot entry for fast on/off at access checkpoints, hood storage in collar for quick deployment in acid rain.
what_it_says: No company owns this person today. Maybe tomorrow, maybe not. The stenciled lot number means they know which crews to show up for and which to avoid. The paracord back splice means they have chrome they paid for themselves, not company-issue, and they've adapted their own gear around it. Independent. Capable. Underpaid and aware of it.
worn_by: former company workers running their own book
manufacturer: Assembled — jacket from Dockline Surplus (street label), henley from Coldwall, trousers from Ironpass (generic run), boots aftermarket composite, belt custom-rigged
price_range: Φ290–Φ420 (assembled piecemeal over time; individual items range Φ40–Φ150)
story_hooks: The stenciled crew number on the sleeve matches a lot designation that was officially decommissioned after a dock collapse that killed eleven workers — someone is still using that designation, and someone is answering it.

An independent hauler in this kit shows up at a job site with cargo that doesn't match any manifest. They were hired through three layers of anonymous relay contracts and have no idea what they're carrying.

The paracord back lacing is a specific knot pattern used by a particular off-grid augmentation clinic as an informal identifier — a way for their clients to recognize each other without saying a word.

physical_description.visual_profile: A compact, utilitarian silhouette built for repetitive heavy labor. The figure reads as grounded and functional—broad across the shoulders, tapered at the ankles. The jacket dominates visually, giving an impression of durability and wear-readiness. The stenciled orange triangle on the left sleeve breaks the monochrome palette and signals affiliation or jurisdiction. Overall impression: street-tier independent worker, self-assembled kit, no corporate branding.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed through the chest and shoulders with intentional room in the thighs for crouching and bending. The henley is fitted enough to layer but not constrictive. Trousers are cut wide at the hip-thigh, tapering slightly toward the ankle. Boots are chunky and grounded. Everything designed for 12-hour shifts, not aesthetics.
physical_description.primary_material: Faded waxed cotton jacket (street-surplus); heavyweight charcoal cotton henley; navy canvas work trousers; grey knit wool balaclava; composite-rubber dock boots with steel toe caps
physical_description.texture: The jacket has a weathered, creased waxed-cotton surface with visible softening at stress points. The henley is dense and slightly nubby. Canvas trousers show a broken-in surface with subtle fading at the knees and seat. Balaclava is tightly knitted, slightly pilled from use. Boots are scuffed grey at the toe, showing underlying composite beneath the wear.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dominant navy (jacket, trousers) and charcoal (henley) create a low-contrast base. Grey knit cap with a single faded orange horizontal stripe. The stenciled orange triangle on the left sleeve (dock-lot mark) is the only bright accent. Boot toe caps weathered to light grey. Overall palette is industrial and drained of color.
physical_description.closures: Jacket: five-button front plus concealed hidden snap placket; two chest flap pockets with reinforced bar-tack stitching; hood collapsed into collar with friction fit. Henley: three-button placket. Trousers: zip fly with reinforced bartack stitching, two front pockets, cargo pockets on both legs with flap closures. Belt: heavy-duty friction-fit webbing with D-ring riveted attachment. Boots: side-zip entry with reinforced eyelets.
distinctive_features: Spinal-rig accommodation channel: back panel slit along spine and re-laced with industrial paracord to allow for spinal augmentation gear or load-bearing exoskeleton harness integration
Hand-stenciled orange triangle with number on left sleeve (dock lot designation, crew mark, or union section ID)
Chest pockets reinforced with street-sewn bar tacks indicating frequent high-load carry
Knee pad channels with pads currently inserted (removable, replaceable)
Wide webbing belt with heavy D-ring attachment point; carries hook tool, work-lamp clip, battered multi-use utility holster
Paracord re-lacing on jacket spine visible from back
Balaclava worn pulled back as watch cap; faded orange stripe indicates either crew affiliation or age-wear
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 4–5 boundary. No corporate issuing, no warranty branding. Every piece selected for function and durability, not status. Assembled from street-label surplus and generic industrial runs. The custom spinal-rig accommodation suggests either personal augmentation investment or frequent work with exoskeleton systems.
physical_description.cultural_context: Independent dock labor, gig-economy freight handler, day-hire autonomous-cargo assistant. Someone who works across multiple small operations, never long enough to get a company uniform. The kit signals: reliable, augmentation-aware, self-maintained, crew-adjacent but not institutionally loyal. No corpo affiliation; possibly union-adjacent or informal collective-member. Willing to customize gear for personal needs.
physical_description.condition_typical: Deliberately worn. Not pristine; not destroyed. The jacket is broken in but well-maintained. Boots scuffed at toe caps from concrete and steel dock surfaces. Canvas trousers show patina at stress points but no major holes or tears. The paracord re-lacing is recent enough to be functional, old enough to be trusted. Everything smells like salt water, grease, and industrial disinfectant.
